title: Sikhism: share
hookLine: share what you earn with others

cards: A father gives his teenage son twenty rupees, a real sum, and sends him to the market with one instruction: make a good deal. Buy something you can sell for a profit. Learn the family business.
On the road the boy meets a group of holy men who haven't eaten in days. He spends every rupee on food for them, and comes home empty-handed. His father is furious.
The boy is calm: he made the truest deal there is. The boy was the young Nanak.

teach.b: That story, like yesterday's, comes from the janamsakhis, and Sikhs call it sacha sauda, the true bargain. A gurdwara stands today where tradition says it happened.
It's a picture of the third pillar of Sikh life: vand chhakna, to share and consume together. Vand means dividing, sharing out. Chhakna means eating, partaking.
Share what you have, then enjoy it, together.
The three pillars fit: remember the name, earn honestly, share what you earn.

Yesterday's hymn at Ang 1245 holds the last two in one breath: the one who eats what he earns by his own effort, and gives some of it away, recognizes the path. Honest work without sharing can turn into hoarding.
Sharing without honest work isn't really yours to give. Sikhs made this concrete.

Sikh tradition asks for dasvandh, setting aside a tenth of one's income for the community and those in need, a practice that grew under the later Gurus. Sharing also means time and skill, not only money.
Sikhs call selfless service seva, and you'll see it in any gurdwara: people cleaning shoes, sweeping floors, chopping onions, who may spend the rest of the week as doctors, drivers or shopkeepers.

A kitchen where everyone eats together is tomorrow's story. Underneath it all, everything comes from the one creator of three days ago, so nothing is entirely private property. Sharing isn't charity from above.
It's handing around what was always meant to go around.

how: Many Sikhs set aside dasvandh, a tenth of their income, for the community and those in need, and give time as seva in the gurdwara, from cleaning to cooking for the shared meal.

o: sharing what you earn, and eating together
fasting one day each week for the poor
giving away everything you own at once

games.q: sharing in Sikh life — tap the pairs.

s: in the story, young Nanak made a profitable trade at the market
he spent the money feeding hungry holy men: the true bargain.
Sikh tradition asks for a tenth of income
dasvandh, for the community and those in need.
Sikh sharing is only about money
seva, service of time and skill, is part of it too.

games.q: your father gives you twenty rupees to make a good deal. on the road you meet hungry holy men. what do you do?
o: buy goods to sell for profit.
spend it all on food for them.
give them a little and keep the rest.
games.why: in the janamsakhi story, young Nanak feeds them with all of it and calls it the true bargain, sacha sauda.

practice: Think of what you'll eat today, and who you could share it with: a coworker at lunch, a neighbor, a friend who's struggling, a stranger outside the shop. Picture handing it over, and eating together if you can.
Notice any reluctance, and let it soften.

wordCard.voice: Vand chhakna. Share and partake: the third pillar of Sikh life, giving some of what you honestly earn. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: share it. Earned honestly, then handed around. That's day two hundred seventy-seven.
